questions.question: Which parts of the key contract does spec 054 own, compared with 004 and 051?

options.label: 054 owns the domain (Recommended)
options.description: 054 states the function from an input string to a canonical key or a refusal, including step precedence, the store's root spellings, the alphabet and the backend profiles. PATH-002 to PATH-007 move into 054 with their IDs unchanged, as BK-456 stage two did, so their existing tests keep their marks. 004 keeps the RemotePath value object (PATH-001, PATH-008 to PATH-017), and its constructor links to 054. 051 keeps the tree, and its Layering paragraph points at 054 instead of 004.

options.label: 054 mints new KEY- IDs
options.description: Same split, but every clause gets a new KEY-NNN ID. PATH-002 to PATH-007 become [DEPRECATED] stubs pointing at 054, and the tests are re-marked. This means more churn and two IDs per fact during the change.

options.label: 054 adds only what is new
options.description: 004 keeps its normaliser and gains a step order. 054 states only the alphabet, the store root spellings and the backend profiles, and links to 004. This is the smallest change, but the key domain is split over two specs.

questions.question: Portable key set, and what happens to a key a backend cannot store (your points 2 and 3)?

options.label: Floor + declared refusals (Recommended)
options.description: The store refuses only what no wire can carry: NUL and lone surrogates, on every backend (so Memory changes too). Every backend must accept a stated portable floor: POSIX portable filename characters, segment and key byte bounds. A key outside the floor but inside the domain can be refused only with InvalidPath, under a profile 054 names (POSIX segment bytes, Windows-forbidden names, object-store key bytes), and with no observable change to the store. That last part is an outcome, not a requirement to check before I/O.

options.label: No floor, declared refusals
options.description: The domain is the same and refusals work the same way, but no set of keys is guaranteed on every backend. Simpler to state and test, but a caller cannot know which keys are portable.

options.label: Fixed alphabet everywhere
options.description: The store refuses anything outside a fixed portable alphabet and length bound, on every backend, before I/O. This is the most portable option, but it breaks existing keys that use spaces, non-ASCII characters or ':' on S3, Memory and others.

questions.question: How should root spellings at the store level relate to BE-029's root spellings at the backend level?

options.label: Two levels, store widens (Recommended)
options.description: At the store, every input that normalises to the empty key is the root. That includes '', '.', './', '/' and '//', plus '\' if backslash is still folded. Folder-shaped calls answer for the root and file-shaped calls refuse. BE-029 keeps its backend-level set, and 054 links to it. Today Store refuses './' and '/', so code breaks this clause: no mark yet, gap recorded under Rule 7.

options.label: Two levels, store stays narrow
options.description: At the store only '' and '.' are the root. Every other input that normalises to empty is InvalidPath on every call. This matches the code and the STORE-002 tests, but '/a' becomes 'a' while '/' is refused.

options.label: One rule, BE-029's six
options.description: The store root set is exactly BE-029's six slash-and-dot spellings. '\' and other inputs are refused, so the root has to be decided before the backslash fold. It agrees with RootPath.dfy, but the precedence becomes order-dependent.

questions.question: What should spec 054 say about backslash, which is folded to '/' today and so makes `a\b` unaddressable?

options.label: Keep the fold, state it (Recommended)
options.description: '\' folds to '/' as the first step, ahead of the '..' and NUL refusals in precedence, so 'a\..\b' is refused. This matches the code, the PATH-002 tests and migration.md ('A Store turns a backslash into / first'). 054 states that `a\b` is outside the store's addressable set, as 051 and BE-032 A.2 already say.

options.label: Refuse it
options.description: InvalidPath for any '\' at the store, the same rule as BE-030 on the kernel. This removes the silent alias of a\b onto a/b, but breaks callers who pass Windows-style paths. The code breaks the clause today, so the gap is recorded.

options.label: Pass it through as a name char
options.description: `a\b` becomes a one-segment name and addressable, and backends that cannot store it refuse under a profile. It conflicts with BE-030's kernel refusal, so 053 would have to change, which is outside this PR's scope.
